posts.name: Kuppy
posts.text:
I get it, there are nuances for tech-bros who are deep in the weeds. Everyone has an anecdote about why I’m wrong. 

Take a step back and be a commodity-bro who’s seen enough supply/demand cycles. Tokens are a commodity. Currently, the token factories are out-stripping token demand. Pricing is the adjustment factor. Except token factories are mostly fixed-price businesses. They have take-or-pay. They have commitments. They will produce tokens at a loss rather than turn off. 

I’m not saying that token demand is slowing. It’s still growing at astronomical rates. I’m saying that token production is now out-pacing demand. The cycle will turn when demand accelerates or token production slows. There’s like half a trillion $ of GPUs waiting to be installed. I don’t think token production slows anytime soon. 

Yeah, I get it. Jevon’s and all. It’s great for AI consumers and innovators. But the guys owning token factories are gonna all go bust in the process, and that’s like $2T of capex to date. You cannot even restructure these things and crush the debt. They’re just stranded by new, and more efficient chips. They’re always going to be stranded by new chips. More efficient Models will strand the more expensive ones. It’s a race to the bottom against fixed costs. It’s the most godawful business misallocation I’ve seen in a while. Makes the Chinese look like prudent capital allocators🤣🤣

It’s like having iron rails when the new railroads run on steel. This bankruptcy cycle will be epic…

quoted.text:
In a normal functioning ecosystem, when the price of tokens drops below the cost of production, the quantity of tokens declines to normalize with pricing. In this case, nothing in AI has any unit economics and you don’t see normalization because everyone is still going full-speed ahead with external funding. (Sort of like shale oil in 2016-2019). Meanwhile, compute prices are based on LT contracts that were signed at above market prices, and are now capital destructive. They’ll eventually catch down to token prices in free-fall.

What we’re seeing here is spot price negatively diverging from term pricing. Usually, when this happens in a cyclical industry, it’s INCREDIBLY BEARISH. Especially when there are take-or-pay contracts that make it difficult to ration supply at prices below cost. What we’re witnessing is a world where losses will accelerate, just as more supply comes online….

posts.name: Lance Breitstein 🇺🇸🌎
posts.text:
DO TECHNICALS PREDICT THE FUTURE AND “FRONTRUN” NEWS?

Over the last year or two, I think I’ve done a decent job calling out some pivotal moments in the market with a pretty solid hit rate. The top in BTC, the top in quantum/froth, the DRAM crack, among others.

I don’t delete tweets or cherry-pick my calls, and I’m certainly wrong plenty of times and take losses like everyone else. In my course, there’s a full record of my market thoughts, documented in my weekly market prep videos.

So what exactly does that mean? And perhaps more importantly, what doesn’t it mean?

First, no trader knows what’s going to happen. Everything is probabilistic at best and total noise at worst. But there are specific moments in time when the odds can become meaningfully skewed in one direction.

I don’t believe technicals somehow “frontrun” the news. What I believe is that technicals help reveal the prevailing sentiment of the market, and that sentiment is the lens through which new information gets interpreted.

Think about it.

Why did semis sell off alongside SKHY on its earnings? And why did SKHY respond so poorly to its numbers? To some degree, because sentiment was already rolling over, and that deterioration was showing up in the charts.

Why does the market suddenly sell off so aggressively on a hot inflation print? Because investors have grown increasingly concerned about oil prices, persistent inflation, and what those pressures mean for interest rates.

Why aren’t we seeing the same enthusiastic responses to positive AI headlines that we saw previously? Because investor sentiment has shifted. People are growing increasingly skeptical of the enormous spending and whether the eventual returns will justify it.

As a dumb day trader, it’s impossible for me to fully understand any one of these themes, let alone all of them. But what my experience and expertise in technical analysis allow me to do is read the collective footprints of the market’s largest participants, expressed through price action.

Those footprints can reveal changes in positioning, conviction, and risk appetite well before the underlying narrative becomes obvious to everyone else.

And that’s what makes technical analysis so powerful to me.

Price action can tell you that something is changing, even when you don’t fully understand why it’s changing. It can reveal that buyers are becoming less aggressive, that good news is no longer being rewarded, or that sellers are gaining control.

None of those observations guarantees what happens next. But when multiple pieces of evidence begin pointing in the same direction, the odds can become increasingly favorable.

I don’t believe technicals predict the future. I believe they provide a window into changing market sentiment, which influences how the market responds to whatever comes next.

And if you’re able to recognize those subtle shifts before they become obvious, you can sometimes find moments where the probabilities are meaningfully in your favor.

posts.name: Tobias Carlisle
posts.text:
The stock market is a forecasting machine. Prices reflect what investors collectively expect profits to be over many years, not what the economy is doing today.
When the outlook stops deteriorating, even while current conditions remain dire, prices can turn sharply higher.
The clearest evidence is the gap between the market’s low and the worst point for jobs.
In every recession since 1970, the stock market bottomed before unemployment peaked. The typical lead was about seven months. In 1990–92, the market had been recovering for nearly two years before the jobless rate topped out.

THEY SAY INFLATION IS 3.7%. FERTILISER IS UP 60%. WHEAT IS UP 35%. GAS IS UP 34%.

Guess which number made the news.

This morning's inflation report says prices rose 0.6% in one month. 3.7% over the year.

Now look at what you actually paid more for.
Gasoline, up 34.2% in a year.
Energy, up 20.4%.
Airfares, up 22.4%.

Gas alone was "over half" of September's rise. Their words, not mine.

The report says groceries are up just 1.8%. Enjoy that number. It's about to change.

The UN's world food price index just hit its highest level since 2022. Cereal prices are up 17% in a year.

Here's the part nobody on the news connects.

Guess where a third of the world's traded urea fertiliser ships through.

The Strait of Hormuz.

Since the war with Iran started in late February, urea exports from the countries that ship through it fell 83% in a year. Ammonia fell 75%. Those are the UN trade agency's April numbers.

Qatar suspended urea production. Iran halted ammonia.

By April urea cost about 80% more than in February. The World Bank expects it to average about 60% higher this year.

And NOAA gives better than even odds of a very strong El Niño this winter. Cocoa, coffee and sugar are in its path.

Farmers pay for fertiliser before they plant. You pay for it at the checkout, months later. Analysts expect the bigger hit in 2027.

So when they tell you inflation is under control, ask which number they mean. The one they quote, or the one you pay?

The implications for the Fed:

-All eyes will now be on Warsh's Q&A at the IMF meetings in Thailand (11:30 pm Eastern time US on Thursday). Markets aren't sure where to price October odds, which moved up to 50%.

-The Fed minutes and some high-profile Fed speak had indicated the bar to raise rates at consecutive meetings, in October, was higher than the market thought it was. Would one report change that? You could argue it either way: No, the Fed doesn't want to look like it is over-reacting to one data point; it wants to focus on broader trends. But the broader trend after this report doesn't look great and raises the question: If you think higher rates are needed, why wait.

-At a minimum, it reinforces the case for going again in December, lest there was any doubt about it. https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-cpi-inflation-10-14-2026/card/nick-timiraos-hot-inflation-reading-bolsters-case-for-another-fed-rate-increase-S9HyA3tQqgUbqCnSJC8R

posts.text:
Yes, another great podcast! 🎙️

This time, I had the pleasure of joining @pahueg on Less Noise More Signal for an inspiring conversation about the global economy, mounting debt, and the future of investing.

We didn't hold back:

→ Why France is Europe's weakest link
→ Why the ECB may have no choice but to step in again
→ How governments are using inflation to escape their debt trap
→ Why holding cash and bonds means destroying your purchasing power
→ Why Europe is losing its economic edge
And, of course, why we're betting on scarcity through quality equities, physical gold, and bitcoin in the Blokland Smart Multi-Asset Fund.

Big thanks to @pahueg for having me and for a great conversation!

Check out the full episode! 👇

posts.name: Holger Zschaepitz
posts.text: Good Morning from Germany, where Berlin is pushing for EU quotas on Chinese chemicals, machinery, and potentially pharmaceuticals, Bloomberg reports. The German trade deficit w/China has hit a record of more than €108bn. Europe’s export powerhouse now wants tougher import barriers. The planned annual cap of 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars would be just the start. Germany wants proposals for more sectors by year-end. https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-14/germany-to-push-eu-to-impose-caps-on-additional-chinese-imports?srnd=homepage-europe
